strengths: Significance: PMVB addresses a useful practical problem: incorporating predictions into commercial MIP solvers through added cardinality constraints. The construction requires little integration effort, and solving all four complementary subproblems preserves exactness independently of prediction quality.

Empirical merits: The evaluation covers logistic regression, GNN and LP predictions, two commercial solvers, several combinatorial problems, and unit commitment. Table 2 reports 1.11–1.31× speedups for exact solving, suggesting potentially useful benefits beyond finding good incumbents.

Presentation and originality: The manuscript clearly distinguishes prediction from solver integration and heuristic use from exhaustive branching. Connecting aggregate prediction errors to neighborhood sizes is an interesting perspective on established local-branching mechanisms.

Reproducibility, limitations and ethics: The manuscript provides a code link, dataset references, hardware information and several solver settings. It explicitly acknowledges the strong independence assumption and possible infeasibility of the data-free restrictions. No material research-ethics concerns are evident from the described experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 2.1 is not established by the stated assumptions. Lemma 2.1 bounds population classification error, but Equation (4) treats this as an accuracy guarantee after selecting variables into U or L using their predictions. A classifier can be accurate overall while all its positive predictions are wrong. Furthermore, A4 concerns independence for fixed ξ, whereas the proof applies concentration to outputs sharing a random instance; the required independence is not established. These gaps undermine the central probability guarantee.

Soundness and practical calibration: Theorem 3.1 follows from Chebyshev’s inequality given valid population means and a variance upper bound, but the experiments do not specify how σ is obtained or validated, especially in the data-free setting. The stronger constraints in Remark 3.1 require additional calibration to inherit a probability guarantee. Section 5.2 uses δ = 0.8, providing only 20% guaranteed coverage for each inequality and no nontrivial joint guarantee. Empirical coverage measurements and a reproducible calibration procedure are needed.

Additional technical gaps: Theorem 4.1 bounds how many LP-selected variables are discarded, but its bound for newly selected variables does not follow merely by complementarity: knapsack solutions can select different numbers of items. Section 3.2 also reverses the pruning condition. If the preferred region excludes every global optimum, at least one complementary region remains feasible under the incumbent objective cut. These arguments need correction, although exhaustive solution of the four regions remains a valid algorithm.

Evaluation: The large heuristic speedups in Section 5.2 measure time to an objective chosen from PMVB’s own 120-second trajectory. This is informative about those targets but does not establish superiority in solution quality under a common budget or time to optimality. Handling of unreached targets, unsuccessful restricted solves, and prediction overhead is insufficiently specified. Fixed-budget gaps or primal integrals, complete online timings, and uncertainty estimates would strengthen the evidence; the SCUC experiments use only five test instances per setting.

Evaluation and significance: Section 5.4 reduces 132 MIPLIB instances to 57 after excluding cases where the restricted problem is immediately infeasible or both methods time out. Excluding PMVB infeasibility omits an important failure mode, so the reported 16% improvement supports a claim limited to the selected subset. Report outcomes for all instances, exclusion counts by reason, and the cost of a practical fallback. Table 4’s coarsely rounded objectives also do not substantiate the claim that optimality is rarely compromised.

Originality and attribution: Prediction-centered restrictions, local branching and multivariable branching are already represented in the cited literature, including [13], [14] and [23]. Comparisons against unmodified solvers do not isolate the contribution of the proposed statistical threshold selection. Baselines using the same predictions with conventional local branching, variable fixing or warm starts, together with threshold ablations, are needed to establish the specific advance.

Reproducibility and presentation: The MKP generator in Section 5.1 sets capacities proportional to (1/(4n)) times the row sum. With the stated positive weights and 10 or 30 constraints, this would almost always leave only the all-zero solution feasible, conflicting with the reported difficult MKP instances; the formula or experimental description needs clarification. Solver versions, random seeds and important training details are not reported in the manuscript. Table 4 contains only 30 entries, including a duplicated blp-ar98, despite the stated evaluation of 57 instances.
